prize_parts.citation: for the experimental discovery of large tunnel magnetoresistance at room temperature in magnetic tunnel junctions

statement.case_for: I keep B005 as my preferred part, but I have narrowed it to the two experimenters whose names I can attach to the original observation. In 1995 Moodera and Miyazaki, independently and within months, showed that spin-dependent tunnelling gives a sizeable resistance change at room temperature, which turned Julliere's 1975 low-temperature result into a usable effect. That is a single, bounded, experimentally verified discovery, reproduced for three decades with a stable interpretation, and it underlies read heads, sensors and magnetic memory. It is also a different physical mechanism from the metallic GMR effect honoured in 2007. It is the kind of finished, original experiment that the statutes ask for. I do not claim it is the most exciting candidate on our list, only that it is the one where I am surest of the topic and of who did the work first.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection that I raised myself in round 1 has not been answered, and I now accept it for Parkin. His name rests on the MgO-barrier step, which was reached in parallel with Yuasa and Djayaprawira, and the coherent-tunnelling theory of Butler and Mathon cannot be represented by the credited names. I cannot be absolutely sure of that priority from the record before us, so I have dropped Parkin and anchored the citation on 1995. The price is that the later giant effect that made the technology real is no longer in the citation. Olle Eriksson's point that this sits close to the 2007 prize in spin electronics remains a fair reading, and the weak opening support (only Olle and I ranked it) tells me that a colleague who weighs maturity and breadth differently could reasonably prefer B021, B024 or B020.

responses.point: Olle ranked B005 fourth, regards it as a continuation of the spin-electronics line of 2007, and notes that Yuasa, Djayaprawira, Butler and Mathon sit outside the credited names.
responses.response: I take the attribution part of this fully and it has changed my configuration: I have removed Parkin and now credit only Moodera and Miyazaki for the 1995 room-temperature discovery, which avoids the unresolved MgO priority question altogether. On the continuation point I still disagree. GMR is a metallic multilayer effect with spin-dependent scattering, whereas TMR is spin-dependent tunnelling across an insulating barrier, with its own physics and a different experimental route, so the discovery was not a variation on Fert and Gruenberg. I also understand your answer on B021: eight years of replication across transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy is substantial, and I would not oppose it. My hesitation is only that a field that has not yet explained its own superconductivity is a harder case for the 'absolutely sure' standard than a settled one.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth holds B020 as a mature programme in which the Mott transition and single-site imaging were themselves the discovery, in answer to the worry that the doped Hubbard payoff has not arrived.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 question in part, and I take it seriously: the superfluid-to-Mott transition seen by Greiner and Bloch is a single, original and verified experiment, and I would accept that as a discovery about nature and not only a platform. My remaining difficulty is the citation. The credit string has to carry the Jaksch-Zoller proposal, the Mott observation, fermionic work and microscopy, and any three names omit someone whose original contribution is on the record, with Jaksch and Hansch outside the list altogether. If the committee could confine the citation to the Mott transition and name Bloch and Greiner with one more, I would find B020 much easier, and it stays one of my alternatives in spirit even though I list B021 and B024 on the ballot because they are cleaner on the three-name limit.

responses.point: Stefan holds that a new measurement capability is itself the achievement, and that Katori and Ye are a clean two-person pair for the lattice clock.
responses.response: I am moved by the instrument argument, which is the part of my own outlook closest to yours, and I rate B024 as a confirmed result across JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE. But my reading of the mandate is that the prize goes to the original idea and first realisation. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration are that. Ye's work taking the clock to 10^-18 is excellent, but it is an optimisation of an existing scheme, which is exactly the second-best experiment the mandate says should not be preferred. You have said you have not verified the priority split, and neither have I. The close precedent of 2005 and 2012 and the pending redefinition of the second make me keep B024 as an alternative and not as my first position.

responses.point: Ulf prefers B025 as the one candidate where a decisive observation settled a thirty-year puzzle, and the chair asked what extra evidence would move him on the optical afterglow credit.
responses.response: I agree that B025 is mature and that it is a discovery about nature, and in that sense it fits the mandate better than the clocks. My problem is the same one I pose for TMR: I cannot be absolutely sure of the names. The BeppoSAX localisation by Costa and Frontera and the optical and redshift work are separable original contributions, van Paradijs cannot be credited, and Groot and others are outside three names. For my own B005 position, the evidence that would move me is a clear record that Parkin's MgO result preceded or matched Yuasa's, which I have not seen, and I would ask Ulf for the corresponding record on the optical afterglow before I could join him.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts TMR as sufficiently distinct from the 2007 GMR prize, and whether it can accept a two-name prize when most members prefer a field with more standing.
Priority between Parkin and the Yuasa and Djayaprawira groups for the large MgO-barrier effect; by removing Parkin I avoid the question but also drop the later development from the citation.
Whether Moodera and Miyazaki are in fact the earliest room-temperature observations, which I know from memory and have not verified against the original papers.
Whether B021 is mature enough given the unsettled pairing mechanism, and whether eight years of replication is enough for the 'absolutely sure' standard.
Whether B020 can be tied to one original experiment (the Mott transition) with a defensible set of three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B005. I have no known connection to Moodera or Miyazaki and none to Parkin, whom I have dropped in any case. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and Bernhard Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg department, but neither is tied to this candidate or to B021 or B024. My TEM collaborations with Japanese microscopy groups are not a connection to Miyazaki or to any shortlisted candidate. My disclosure is otherwise unchanged from round 1.
